'''Emil Thomas Kaiser''' (February 15, 1938 – July 18, 1988) was a Hungarian-born American biochemist.<ref name="NYT">{{cite news|work=[[The New York Times]]|title=Dr. Emil Kaiser, 50, Researcher of Proteins|date=July 20, 1988|page=8}}</ref><ref name="CTR">{{cite news|url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1988-07-20-8801160412-story.html|work=[[Chicago Tribune]]|title=Biochemical Researcher Emil Thomas Kaiser, 50|last=Heise|first=Kenan|date=July 20, 1988|accessdate=November 2, 2022}}</ref><ref name="NAP">{{cite book|url=http://www.nap.edu/readingroom.php?book=biomems&page=ekaiser.html|publisher=[[National Academies Press]]|title=Emil Thomas Kaiser|series=Biographical Memoirs|year=1997|volume=72|last=Westheimer|first=F. H.|pages=219–229}}</ref>
Kaiser was most notable for his research of [[enzyme]] modification.<ref name="CTR"/>

He also was noted for developing new types of [[catalysts]] and for a more active form of a [[peptide hormone]].<ref name="CTR"/>

[[Chicago Tribune]] said that Kaiser "developed a whole new approach to synthetic chemistry".<ref name="CTR"/>

[[Joshua Lederberg]], a Nobel laureate and president of Rockefeller University in New York, said that Kaiser's research of "synthetic enzymes and other [[polypeptides]] advanced basic scientific understanding in ways that had important implications for medicine".<ref name="CTR"/>

Kaiser was the Louis Block Professor at the University of Chicago,<ref name="NYT"/> the Patrick E. and Beatrice M. Haggerty Professor at Rockefeller University,<ref name="NYT"/> a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]],<ref name="NYT"/> the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]],<ref name="NYT"/> the [[National Institutes of Health]]<ref name="NYT"/> and the [[National Science Foundation]].<ref name="NYT"/>

==Life and career==
Kaiser was born in [[Budapest]], [[Hungary]]. He graduated from the [[University of Chicago]] with a B.S. degree,  and received his Ph.D. from [[Harvard University]].<ref name="NYT"/>
He joined the faculty of the [[University of Chicago]] in 1963, and advanced to the Louis Block Professorship in 1981. He moved to the [[Rockefeller University]] in 1982.<ref name="NYT"/>
